beats.text: A shared counter says five items are in the buffer.
The producer adds an item, and runs count plus plus. The consumer takes one, and runs count minus minus.
One in, one out. Count should still be five.
But each line is three machine steps: load count into a register, change the register, store it back.
The producer loads five, and adds one. Its register says six.
Then the consumer gets the CPU. It loads count, still five, and subtracts one. Its register says four.
The producer stores six.
The consumer stores four. Count is now four. An item has vanished.
Swap the last two stores, and count ends at six. Only five is right.
When the result depends on the order in which processes touch shared data, that is a race condition.
The fix starts with a name. The code that touches shared data is the critical section: a room only one process may be in.
A process asks to enter in its entry section, and leaves through its exit section.
A correct solution needs three things. Mutual exclusion: only one process inside at a time.
Progress: if the room is empty and someone wants in, the choice cannot be put off forever.
Bounded waiting: once you ask, the others can go before you only a limited number of times.
Peterson's solution does it in software, for two processes, with two variables.
flag of i says: I want to enter. turn says whose turn it is.
Each process raises its flag, then politely gives the turn away, and waits while the other wants in and has the turn.
If both try at once, turn can hold only one value. Whoever wrote it last, waits. So only one gets in.
On modern processors, instructions can be reordered, so Peterson also needs a memory barrier.
For the exam.
count plus plus is load, change, store.
From five, the race gives four or six.
Mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting.
Peterson: flag and turn.
